before.claim: Replication precedes cell division because each daughter cell requires an inherited copy of the DNA base sequence. Accurate sequence copying allows the new cells in a growing root, a healing wound or a dividing bacterium to retain the genetic instructions of the parent cell. It does not mean that replication is perfectly error-free; rare mistakes can persist as mutations.

The DNA sequence serves as an ordered template. Replication copies the whole DNA molecule; transcription later uses selected DNA regions to produce RNA. Keeping these processes distinct explains how a cell can preserve genes while changing which genes it expresses.

Follow the consequence: an unreplicated chromosome contains one DNA double helix; a correctly replicated chromosome contains two identical sister chromatids. Copying sequence information first makes it possible for division to supply each future daughter nucleus with the same instructions. In an ordinary cell cycle this copying occurs during S phase, before mitosis—not during cytokinesis.

after.claim: DNA replication produces copies with the same base sequence as the original DNA. It is required for reproduction and for growth and tissue replacement in multicellular organisms, so new cells inherit genetic instructions. Copying is highly accurate, though rare errors can persist as mutations.

Replication copies DNA into DNA; transcription uses a selected DNA region to make RNA. Replication preserves genetic information for new cells, whereas transcription allows that information to be expressed.

before.claim: The two parental DNA strands separate. Each becomes a template for synthesis of a complementary new strand, producing two double helices that each contain one original strand and one newly made strand. This arrangement is called semi-conservative, not conservative or dispersive.

A pairs with T and G with C. Each exposed parental base therefore helps select the corresponding nucleotide for the new strand. DNA polymerase also contributes to accuracy through nucleotide selection and, where present, proofreading; complementary base pairing by itself does not make replication infallible.

Imagine a parental DNA duplex with one strand 5′-ATGC-3′ and the complementary strand 3′-TACG-5′. Once the strands separate, complementary nucleotides are added opposite each template base, so each new partner has the same sequence as the partner displaced from the original duplex. The outcome is not one wholly old double helix and one wholly new helix: both daughter molecules contain one conserved parental strand. Complementarity explains sequence fidelity, while proofreading makes copying more accurate still.

after.claim: The two parental DNA strands separate. Each is a template for a complementary new strand. Each daughter double helix therefore contains one original strand and one new strand: replication is semi-conservative.

A pairs with T and G with C, so the template sequence determines the order of nucleotides in the new strand. A template segment TACG produces the complementary segment ATGC. Complementarity allows a high degree of accuracy; it does not mean errors are impossible.

before.claim: Helicase uses energy to unwind the parental double helix and disrupt the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, exposing the two template strands. The sugar–phosphate backbones remain intact at the fork; helicase does not cut the strands into nucleotides.

DNA polymerase reads an exposed template and joins complementary deoxyribonucleotides by forming phosphodiester bonds in the growing daughter strand. In cellular replication it extends a pre-existing 3′ end rather than starting synthesis from nothing. Helicase separates the strands; polymerase builds their complementary copies.

The double helix cannot serve as two separate templates while its bases remain paired internally. Helicase disrupts the hydrogen bonds between paired bases at the fork, making the two parent strands available. DNA polymerase then uses exposed bases to select complementary incoming DNA nucleotides and joins them into the growing strand; it does not unzip the parental helix by itself. The weak interstrand hydrogen bonds are disrupted during unwinding, but the strong covalent sugar–phosphate backbone of each parental strand remains intact.

after.claim: Helicase unwinds the double helix and breaks hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, exposing the two DNA strands. The covalent sugar–phosphate backbones remain intact.

DNA polymerase uses each exposed strand as a template, selecting complementary DNA nucleotides and joining them by covalent phosphodiester bonds to form a new strand. Helicase separates existing strands; DNA polymerase synthesizes their complementary copies.

before.claim: A PCR cycle first heats DNA to separate strands, then lowers the temperature so short DNA primers can anneal to complementary sequences on opposite strands, then allows thermostable Taq DNA polymerase to extend those primers. The chosen primers define the target; repeated cycles can produce many copies of the region. PCR is not the same as replication of an entire chromosome.

DNA has a negatively charged sugar–phosphate backbone, so an electric field draws fragments toward the positive electrode. In an appropriate gel, shorter DNA fragments generally travel farther than longer ones. Compare bands against a DNA ladder to estimate length; a matching band position does not reveal the fragment's complete base sequence.

PCR does not sort DNA fragments: it repeatedly copies a chosen region between two primers. After many cycles the target sequence can be abundant enough to analyse, provided the primers bind as intended and controls exclude contamination. Gel electrophoresis is the distinct separation step. Because DNA carries negatively charged phosphate groups, fragments migrate toward the positive electrode through a porous gel. Under comparable gel conditions, shorter fragments generally travel farther. A band position indicates approximate fragment length, not by itself the identity of a person or disease.

before.claim: Forensic investigations and parentage testing compare informative DNA markers. Amplification makes small samples analysable and gel or capillary separation distinguishes fragment-length patterns. Agreement at one marker is weak evidence; combining multiple independent markers can greatly reduce the chance of a coincidental match.

A DNA-marker match is evidence that two samples may share a source, not certainty about identity. Multiple independent markers reduce coincidental matches, but contamination, close relatives, population frequencies and sample handling still matter to a forensic or parentage conclusion.

Matching loci supports a probabilistic comparison, not the claim that two people must be identical. Testing more independently informative STR markers generally reduces the chance of a coincidental profile match. Contamination, sample quality and population assumptions still matter. Illustrative classroom comparisons must not be presented as observed forensic case data.

PCR can amplify chosen variable DNA regions from a small sample, while electrophoresis subsequently separates the products by fragment length. Similar band positions can support a comparison, but they do not independently prove identity: unrelated people may share fragment sizes, and contamination or mixtures can mislead. Multiple informative genetic markers, reference samples and controls strengthen an inference. For parentage analysis, compare each child's alleles with possible contributions from each parent. Explain what the data rule out and what remains uncertain rather than declaring a perfect match from one gel.

after.claim: PCR amplifies selected DNA regions from small samples. Electrophoresis separates the amplified fragments by length, allowing informative markers to be compared in forensic investigations and paternity testing. In parentage analysis, each child’s alleles must be compatible with contributions from the biological parents.

A match at one marker does not establish identity: different people can share that fragment length. Using more independent markers reduces the probability of a false match. This illustrates how additional measurements increase reliability. Contamination, mixtures, close relatives and sample handling still affect interpretation; classroom profiles are illustrative rather than evidence from a real case.
